summary: Mobile IPv6 signaling between a mobile node and its home agent is normally secured with IPsec and IKE. This experimental RFC proposes an alternative security framework that uses TLS to establish keying material and other bootstrapping information, for Mobile IPv6 and Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6.

eli5.summary: Usually a traveler and home use one special lock. This offers a second kind of lock that lots of programs already know how to use.

subtitle: Alternative security framework for Mobile IPv6 using TLS instead of IPsec

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 standardly uses IPsec and IKE for security between mobile nodes and home agents, but implementations show this coupling is complex and requires modifications to both the IPsec and Mobile IPv6 components.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes using TLS to establish security associations between the mobile node and a Home Agent Controller (HAC). The HAC generates keys and bootstrapping parameters over a TLS-protected tunnel, then the mobile node uses those keys to secure binding management messages and optionally user traffic with the home agent.
tldr.outcome: The approach simplifies implementation and deployment while maintaining equivalent security to IKE/IPsec. TLS is already widely implemented in operating systems, reducing the need for extensive IPsec integration.

today: RFC 6618 is an experimental specification proposing a TLS-based alternative to IPsec for Mobile IPv6 security. It has not superseded the standard IKE/IPsec approach, which remains the normative security architecture for Mobile IPv6. The experimental status allows for implementation and deployment experience with this alternative model.

sections.title: Security Alternatives for Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) enables hosts to move between networks while maintaining connectivity through a home agent that tunnels traffic to the mobile node's current location. The standard security architecture uses IPsec and IKE for establishing and maintaining security associations between the mobile node and home agent.

Implementation experience has shown that integrating IPsec and IKE with Mobile IPv6 is complex. The tight coupling between the protocols requires modifications to both the IPsec stack and the Mobile IPv6 component to handle dynamic IP addresses and changing care-of addresses. This RFC proposes an alternative security framework using Transport Layer Security (TLS), which is already implemented in most operating systems and widely deployed in applications. The approach decouples Mobile IPv6 security from IPsec, reducing implementation complexity.
sections.eli5: The normal way to secure a traveling phone is complicated. This offers a simpler way using a kind of security that is already in your computer.

sections.title: TLS-Based Security Establishment
sections.content:
The architecture introduces a new functional entity called the Home Agent Controller (HAC), which can be co-located with the home agent or be an independent node. The security process has three phases:

First, the mobile node establishes a TLS session with the HAC and authenticates using either a pre-shared key or an EAP method. Second, the HAC generates security parameters and delivers them to the mobile node through the secure TLS tunnel. These parameters include a Security Parameter Index (SPI), encryption and integrity keys for the MN-HA relationship, and the ciphersuite to be used. Third, both the mobile node and home agent use these parameters to secure Mobile IPv6 signaling messages and optionally user plane traffic.

The HAC may proactively push security association information to home agents, or home agents may query the HAC when a mobile node contacts them. All communication between the HAC and HA must be integrity and confidentially protected.
sections.eli5: A middle person called the Home Agent Controller sets up keys using TLS. It gives the same keys to both the traveler and the home agent, so they can talk securely.

sections.title: Security Association and Key Management
sections.content:
Each security association established between a mobile node and home agent contains: a Mobility SPI (Security Parameter Index) assigned by the HAC to identify the SA, MN-HA keys for both directions (one set of encryption keys and one set for integrity), SA validity time (how long the keys remain valid), SA scope (whether it protects signaling only or both signaling and user data), and the selected ciphersuite defining the encryption and integrity algorithms.

The SA is not tied to the mobile node's care-of address, so it remains valid even as the mobile node moves and its address changes. The mobile node must re-contact the HAC before the SA validity time expires to refresh the keys. The home agent can signal to the mobile node that it should re-establish the SA using a dedicated status code in binding acknowledgement messages.
sections.eli5: The keys are special numbers that the HAC creates. They work even if the traveler moves to a different location and gets a new temporary address.

sections.title: MN-to-HAC Request-Response Protocol
sections.content:
Communication between the mobile node and HAC uses a simple lockstep request-response protocol running inside the TLS tunnel. Messages are framed with a version field, identifier (1 to 255 per session), and length. The content is encoded using HTTP-like headers with type-value pairs.

The first request (MHAuth-Init) contains the mobile node's identity and proposed authentication method. The HAC responds with the selected authentication method. The mobile node then provides its authentication credentials (either EAP payloads or proof of knowledge of the pre-shared key). Upon successful authentication, the HAC sends the final response containing the security association parameters, including the SPI, ciphersuite, keys, and bootstrapping information such as the home agent address and home address.
sections.eli5: The traveler asks the controller for keys. The controller checks who they are. If they pass, the controller gives them keys and tells them where the home agent is.

sections.title: Protecting Mobile IPv6 Signaling and Data
sections.content:
Once the mobile node has obtained security parameters from the HAC, binding management messages (Binding Updates and Binding Acknowledgements) and optionally reverse-tunneled user traffic between the mobile node and home agent are protected using the same ciphersuite for both integrity and confidentiality.

All protected packets carry a sequence number to detect replay attacks. The SA scope parameter determines whether protection applies to signaling messages only or to both signaling and user data. If user data is protected, packets without the correct protection are silently discarded. The same algorithms protect traffic in both directions, with independent sequence numbers maintained for each direction.
sections.eli5: Once they have keys, every message from the traveler to home agent and back is locked using those keys. They also number the messages to catch cheaters trying to replay old messages.
